description:
We're a two-person team from Kazakhstan, passionate about AI, software engineering, and space exploration!

Our strengths include Python, backend and full-stack development, machine learning, and building real-world applications.

Our mission is to turn NASA's open data into something innovative, useful, and technically impressive.

Just two curious minds, a lot of code, and one big mission: reach for the stars! 🚀🐈
summary: We built a web atlas with an interactive map and a fire activity calendar using NASA FIRMS data. MODIS and VIIRS observe Earth at different resolutions and overpass times, so a change of sensor can appear in the record as an increase in fires. To compare seasons, we count active grid cells on a common grid and convert VIIRS activity to the Aqua/MODIS scale. In our North Kazakhstan Region pilot, this reduced the mean absolute error of monthly estimates against Aqua by about 85% for both Suomi NPP and NOAA‑20 on held-out data from 2024–2025. Users can select an area, compare a month with its historical baseline, and explore relationships with weather and landscape factors. This helps monitoring teams identify periods and locations that warrant a closer look.
details:
We built the MODIS and VIIRS Fire Activity Atlas, a web application for comparing satellite-detected fire activity across seasons. Users can select a territory, compare each month with its historical baseline, and replay daily detections on a map with wind, rainfall, cloud cover, and terrain layers.

MODIS and VIIRS differ in spatial resolution and overpass timing, so a change of sensor can look like an increase in fire activity. We place both sets of observations on the same grid and count each active cell once per UTC day for each satellite. Using dates with standard observations from both sensors, we calculate a factor that converts VIIRS activity to the Aqua/MODIS scale. In North Kazakhstan, we fitted the factors on 2020–2023 data and tested them on 2024–2025 data. On a 2 × 2 km grid, monthly mean absolute error against Aqua fell by about 85% for both Suomi NPP and NOAA‑20.

The atlas connects the calendar, map, and correlation matrix. A user can open an unusual month, locate the detections, and explore how activity varied with weather or landscape factors. Users can also compare their own CSV or Excel data with atlas data. This helps fire monitoring teams and land managers prioritize periods and locations for closer investigation.

We used Python and DuckDB for data processing, JavaScript and Leaflet for the interactive map, and GitHub and Docker for collaboration and deployment. We accounted for detection confidence and known archive gaps, identified the satellite source for each period, and flagged uncertainty about local viewing conditions.
